pharm: Sulfonylurea that lowers blood glucose chiefly by stimulating insulin release from functioning pancreatic beta cells, with additional extrapancreatic effects on chronic use
quick: Start 2.5-5 mg once daily (1.25 mg if sensitive); maintenance 1.25-20 mg/day; max 20 mg/day
Take with breakfast or the first main meal
Not recommended; insulin generally preferred; stop at least 2 weeks before delivery
Caution; some sulfonylureas pass into milk - risk of infant hypoglycemia
Use conservative dosing; impairment raises hypoglycemia risk
Use conservative dosing; impairment raises hypoglycemia risk
Increases hypoglycemia risk; rare disulfiram-like reaction reported
Blood glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c); watch for hypoglycemia
summary: Glibenclamide (US name glyburide) is a second-generation sulfonylurea used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It lowers glucose by stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells and so requires functioning islets. The main hazard is hypoglycemia, which can be severe and prolonged, particularly in the elderly, debilitated, or malnourished and in those with renal or hepatic impairment. The label carries a class warning of possible increased cardiovascular mortality with oral hypoglycemic agents. It is contraindicated in type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, and with bosentan.
indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus - as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults

dosage.t: With breakfast or the first main meal
dosage.n: Patients more sensitive to hypoglycemic drugs should start at 1.25 mg daily

dosage.d: 1.25 to 20 mg/day, single or divided doses
dosage.t: Increase by no more than 2.5 mg at weekly intervals per glucose response
dosage.n: Doses above 10 mg/day may respond better given twice daily; daily doses over 20 mg are not recommended

dosage.t: No transition/priming dose needed except from chlorpropamide
dosage.n: After chlorpropamide, exercise care for the first 2 weeks due to overlapping drug effects and hypoglycemia risk

dosage.t: Withdraw insulin and raise glyburide by 1.25-2.5 mg every 2-10 days
dosage.n: Hypoglycemia may occur during conversion; monitor closely
Also applies to renal or hepatic impairment; assess renal function

admin: Take once daily with breakfast or the first main meal
Doses above 10 mg/day may be split into twice-daily dosing
If co-administered with colesevelam, give glyburide at least 4 hours before colesevelam
Titrate by no more than 2.5 mg per week based on blood glucose response
During stress (fever, trauma, infection, surgery) insulin may need to replace glyburide temporarily
moa: Glibenclamide acutely lowers blood glucose by stimulating insulin release from functioning beta cells in the pancreatic islets, an action dependent on intact islet function. The mechanism on long-term use is less clear: glucose lowering persists despite a gradual decline in measurable insulin secretory response, suggesting extrapancreatic effects also contribute. It also produces a mild diuresis by enhancing renal free-water clearance.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity or allergy to the drug
Diabetic ketoacidosis, with or without coma (treat with insulin)
relative: Elderly, debilitated, or malnourished patients (high hypoglycemia risk)
Renal or hepatic impairment (elevated drug levels and reduced gluconeogenesis)
G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolytic anemia; consider a non-sulfonylurea)
monitor: Signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, especially with deficient caloric intake, exercise, or alcohol
Blood glucose and HbA1c for primary or secondary failure
Liver function if cholestatic jaundice or hepatitis suspected

preg: Glyburide is not recommended for use in pregnancy. Animal reproduction studies in rats and rabbits at doses up to 500 times the human dose showed no evidence of impaired fertility or fetal harm, but there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women (former Pregnancy Category B). Because abnormal maternal blood glucose is linked to a higher incidence of congenital abnormalities, many experts recommend insulin during pregnancy to keep glucose near normal. Prolonged severe neonatal hypoglycemia (4 to 10 days) has been reported in infants of mothers taking a sulfonylurea at delivery; if used, glyburide should be discontinued at least two weeks before the expected delivery date.
lact: It is not known whether glyburide is excreted in human milk, but some sulfonylureas are. Because of the potential for hypoglycemia in a nursing infant, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, accounting for the importance of the drug to the mother. If the drug is stopped and diet alone is inadequate, insulin therapy should be considered.
renal: Renal insufficiency may cause elevated glyburide levels and diminish gluconeogenic capacity, both of which raise the risk of serious, sometimes prolonged hypoglycemia. In patients with impaired renal function the initial and maintenance dosing should be conservative. Elderly patients are prone to renal insufficiency, so dose selection should include assessment of renal function. Glyburide is excreted as metabolites roughly equally in bile and urine.
hepatic: Hepatic insufficiency may elevate glyburide levels and impair gluconeogenesis, increasing the risk of serious hypoglycemia; dosing should be conservative. Cholestatic jaundice and hepatitis may occur rarely and can progress to liver failure - discontinue glyburide if this occurs. Isolated transaminase elevations have also been reported.

major: Bosentan - contraindicated (increased risk of liver enzyme elevations)
NSAIDs and other highly protein-bound drugs, salicylates, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, probenecid, coumarins, MAO inhibitors - potentiate hypoglycemia
Beta-adrenergic blockers - potentiate hypoglycemia and mask its warning signs
moderate: Ciprofloxacin (and other fluoroquinolones) - reported potentiation of hypoglycemia

Thiazides/diuretics, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid products, estrogens, oral contraceptives, phenytoin, nicotinic acid, sympathomimetics, calcium channel blockers, isoniazid - tend to cause hyperglycemia and loss of control
minor: Colesevelam - reduces glyburide AUC/Cmax (separate dosing by at least 4 hours)
Topiramate - modest reductions in glyburide AUC and Cmax
Metformin - variable decreases in glyburide AUC/Cmax of uncertain clinical significance
interactions.food: Take with breakfast or the first main meal; deficient caloric intake increases hypoglycemia risk
interactions.alcohol: Increases the risk of hypoglycemia; disulfiram-like reactions have been reported very rarely
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor blood glucose and HbA1c; observe closely for hypoglycemia when interacting drugs are added and for loss of control when they are withdrawn

common: Gastrointestinal disturbances - nausea, epigastric fullness, heartburn (about 1.8% in trials)
Allergic skin reactions - pruritus, erythema, urticaria, maculopapular eruptions (about 1.5%)
serious: Severe or prolonged hypoglycemia (coma, seizure, neurologic impairment)
Cholestatic jaundice and hepatitis, which may progress to liver failure
Hematologic reactions - leukopenia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, pancytopenia (sulfonylurea class)
rare: Porphyria cutanea tarda and photosensitivity (sulfonylurea class)
Changes in accommodation or blurred vision (glucose-related)
emergency: Severe hypoglycemia with coma, seizure, or neurologic impairment - medical emergency

monitoring: Blood glucose (and urine glucose) to find the minimum effective dose and detect primary/secondary failure
Signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, especially in the elderly and those on beta-blockers
Liver function tests if cholestatic jaundice or hepatitis is suspected
CBC if a blood dyscrasia is suspected
Renal function, particularly in elderly patients
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed with your morning meal; this drug supplements - it does not replace - diet and exercise
Learn the symptoms, treatment, and predisposing conditions for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) and share this with family
Hypoglycemia is more likely with skipped meals, prolonged exercise, alcohol, or combining glucose-lowering drugs
Test urine and/or blood glucose regularly as directed
Report jaundice, dark urine, persistent skin rash, or unusual bleeding or infection promptly
Avoid or limit alcohol; it can lower blood sugar and rarely cause a disulfiram-like reaction
pk: Significant absorption within 1 hour; blood-glucose lowering begins soon after dosing
Peak drug levels at about 4 hours after a dose
Terminal serum half-life about 10 hours (biphasic decline)
Blood-glucose lowering persists about 24 hours after a single morning dose
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep container tightly closed with safety closure
pearls: Glibenclamide is the INN (international nonproprietary name); glyburide is the US adopted name (USAN), and the drug is FDA-approved as glyburide
Requires functioning pancreatic beta cells - ineffective and contraindicated in type 1 diabetes and DKA
Highest hypoglycemia risk among second-generation sulfonylureas in the elderly and in renal/hepatic impairment due to long-acting active metabolites
Class warning of increased cardiovascular mortality is based on the UGDP tolbutamide study
Excreted roughly 50% in bile and 50% in urine - a dual pathway differing from most other sulfonylureas
Consider a non-sulfonylurea in G6PD deficiency because of hemolytic anemia risk
Separate from colesevelam by giving glyburide at least 4 hours earlier
missed: If you miss a dose, take it with food as soon as you remember on the same day. Skip it if it is nearly time for the next dose, and do not take a double dose. Because dosing is tied to a meal, contact your clinician if you frequently miss doses or skip meals, as this affects blood sugar control.
overdose: Overdose produces hypoglycemia. Mild symptoms without loss of consciousness or neurologic findings are treated aggressively with oral glucose plus adjustments in dose and meal timing, with monitoring until the patient is out of danger. Severe reactions with coma, seizure, or other neurologic impairment are medical emergencies requiring immediate hospitalization: give a rapid IV injection of concentrated (50%) glucose followed by a continuous infusion of more dilute (10%) glucose to keep blood glucose above 100 mg/dL. Monitor closely for at least 24 to 48 hours, as hypoglycemia may recur after apparent recovery.
